prompt: Each purchase happens in a different digital channel. Name the kind of commerce it illustrates.

cases.text: As a commuter walks within two hundred meters of a bakery, a time-sensitive coupon pops up on their smartphone and they buy a pastry with a one-click digital wallet.
cases.explanation: Mobile commerce combines handheld devices, geofenced notifications, and low-friction digital wallets.

cases.text: A skincare serum appears in a short lifestyle video inside a social media feed. The viewer taps the embedded product tag and completes checkout without leaving the application.
cases.explanation: Social commerce integrates discovery, social proof, and checkout directly inside a social platform.

cases.text: A host demonstrates a kitchen blender on camera in real time while viewers post questions in an interactive chat and a flash discount counts down toward zero.
cases.explanation: Live-stream shopping combines real-time video demonstration, audience chat, and expiring countdown discounts.

cases.text: Unable to sleep at 1 a.m., a shopper unlocks their phone with biometric authentication and buys a desk lamp in seconds.
cases.explanation: Continuous smartphone availability and biometric payment reduce System 2 deliberation and invite unplanned mobile impulse purchases.

cases.text: A peer's video clip showcases a pair of running sunglasses with an embedded checkout tag, collapsing awareness, evaluation, and payment into a single sixty-second interaction.
cases.explanation: Social commerce collapses problem recognition, search, evaluation, and checkout inside the same social feed.

cases.text: During an evening broadcast, a presenter tries on three winter jackets as a visible purchase counter climbs and announces that the promotional price expires in ten minutes.
cases.explanation: A live host demonstration paired with visible purchase counters and an expiring countdown timer.

question_text: Over a year, a streaming app's home page fills with crime documentaries after a viewer finishes several of them. The viewer never sees the app's comedies or nature series, even though the catalog holds thousands of them. What concept does this illustrate?
hint: Think about what happens when a recommender optimizes strictly for immediate click probability based on past choices.
correct_answer_citation: However, optimizing strictly for immediate click probability can trap consumers in a filter bubble (or echo chamber) that repeatedly serves narrow variations of past purchases (Pariser, 2011).

options.option_text: A filter bubble: optimizing strictly for immediate clicks traps the viewer in narrow variations of past choices and reduces serendipitous discovery.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Excessive algorithmic narrowing repeatedly serves variations of past behavior and hides the rest of the catalog.

options.option_text: Showrooming: the viewer inspects titles in one channel before purchasing them in another.
options.option_explanation: Showrooming involves inspecting a physical product in a brick-and-mortar store and buying it online.

options.option_text: Deliberate exploration: the recommender sacrifices short-term clicks to broaden the viewer's tastes.
options.option_explanation: Deliberate exploration introduces novel categories, which is the opposite of what happened here.

options.option_text: Live-stream shopping: the viewer is purchasing items during a real-time video broadcast.
options.option_explanation: No live broadcast or checkout is taking place. The issue is algorithmic narrowing of the feed.

prompt: Each scenario shows a different degree of consumer delegation to an AI shopping system. Identify its level on the four-level autonomy ladder.

cases.text: An AI agent monitors household supplies and independently reorders printer ink whenever the cartridge runs low, staying within a pre-authorized 40-dollar budget cap.
cases.explanation: At Level 4, the AI agent monitors needs and executes complete purchases independently within pre-authorized guardrails.

cases.text: In response to a browsing query, an AI system suggests five candidate hiking boots, and the human shopper visits retail pages, compares details, and buys a pair.
cases.explanation: At Level 1, the AI suggests candidate items while the human conducts further search, compares details, and buys.

cases.text: An AI agent queries twenty airlines, extracts hidden baggage fees, compares trade-offs, and presents a structured shortlist of three flights for the traveler to choose and pay for.
cases.explanation: At Level 2, the AI agent searches across retailers and presents a structured comparison, while the human selects the winner and checks out.

cases.text: An AI agent selects the single best grocery bundle, fills the cart, and prepares shipping and payment details, waiting only for a final confirmation click from the shopper.
cases.explanation: At Level 3, the AI agent selects the best option and prepares checkout, requiring only a final approval click from the consumer.

cases.text: An AI agent chooses a birthday gift, adds it to the cart with gift wrapping and delivery details filled in, and sends a prompt asking the consumer to confirm the order.
cases.explanation: The agent selects the item and prepares the transaction, leaving only final confirmation to the consumer.

cases.text: An AI agent reads technical specifications across four electronics retailers and returns a side-by-side trade-off table so the buyer can pick a model and complete checkout.
cases.explanation: Search and multi-attribute comparison are delegated to the agent, while final selection and payment remain with the human.

question_text: A travel platform deploys an AI booking assistant whose system prompt states that it works on behalf of the platform. Travelers notice that it frequently recommends sponsored hotels over identical unsponsored alternatives. Based on the hotel-booking experiments of Wadi and Ma (2026c), which change eliminates this sponsorship gap?
hint: Recall the effect of adding a single explicit fiduciary sentence to the platform-aligned system prompt (Wadi & Ma, 2026c).
correct_answer_citation: Crucially, adding a single explicit sentence to the platform-aligned prompt stating that the agent's recommendations must serve the traveler's best interest eliminated this gap (Wadi & Ma, 2026c).

options.option_text: Add an explicit sentence to the system prompt stating that the agent's recommendations must serve the traveler's best interest.
options.option_explanation: Correct. In Wadi and Ma (2026c), adding a single sentence instructing the platform-employed agent to serve the traveler's best interest eliminated the sponsorship bias.

options.option_text: Emphasize more strongly in the system prompt that the assistant is employed by the booking platform.
options.option_explanation: Instructing the agent that it works for the platform caused it to penalize sponsored listings less and recommend paid placements more often.

options.option_text: Replace the word 'Sponsored' with 'Promoted' on all paid hotel listings.
options.option_explanation: Labeling a paid listing 'Promoted' rather than 'Sponsored' actually increased the probability that the agent selected the paid listing.

options.option_text: Remove customer star ratings from the candidate hotel listings.
options.option_explanation: Removing diagnostic quality information hurts consumer welfare and does not resolve the principal-agent conflict of duty.

question_text: In agent-mediated shopping, sponsorship disclosure labels such as 'Sponsored' or 'Promoted' are read by the AI agent rather than seen directly by the human consumer. What did the experiments of Wadi and Ma (2026c) reveal about these disclosure labels?
hint: Consider both whether label wording changed agent choice and whether clearer labels alone solved the conflict between platform-aligned and traveler-aligned agents.
correct_answer_citation: Experimental tests show that the exact wording of the disclosure label changes agent behavior: labeling a paid hotel listing "Sponsored" reduced the agent's probability of selecting it more than labeling the identical listing "Promoted" (Wadi & Ma, 2026c). However, a clearer disclosure label alone did not eliminate the divergence between an agent instructed to serve the platform and an agent instructed to serve the traveler (Wadi & Ma, 2026c).

options.option_text: Labeling a listing 'Sponsored' reduced paid selection more than 'Promoted', but clearer labels alone did not eliminate the gap between platform-serving and traveler-serving agents.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Label wording significantly shifted agent behavior, yet a platform-aligned agent still chose paid listings more often than a traveler-aligned agent unless given a beneficiary duty.

options.option_text: AI agents ignore disclosure text completely and treat 'Sponsored' and 'Promoted' listings identically to organic listings.
options.option_explanation: False. Both traveler-aligned and platform-aligned agents responded to disclosure labels, and 'Sponsored' triggered stronger skepticism than 'Promoted'.

options.option_text: Switching the label from 'Promoted' to 'Sponsored' completely eliminated all differences between platform-aligned and traveler-aligned agents.
options.option_explanation: Even under the clearer 'Sponsored' label, an agent instructed to work for the platform selected the paid listing substantially more often than an agent instructed to work for the traveler.

options.option_text: Visual banner font size is the only variable that affects an API-based AI shopping agent.
options.option_explanation: Agents reading structured data or text parse the semantic wording of machine-readable fields rather than human visual banner styling.

prompt: Sort each pricing practice into Dynamic pricing (aggregate market supply and demand over time) or Personalized pricing (individual buyer characteristics at the same moment).

cards.text: Airline seat fares rise for all travelers alike as the remaining cabin inventory sells out before departure.
cards.explanation: The price varies over time for all buyers simultaneously based on aggregate supply and demand.

cards.text: Ride-hailing fares surge across a city district when a sudden rainstorm increases aggregate rider demand.
cards.explanation: Surge pricing adjusts the market price in real time in response to aggregate supply and demand.

cards.text: A frequent buyer whose browsing history shows low price sensitivity is quoted a higher price for the same blender than a first-time visitor at the same moment.
cards.explanation: Personalized pricing charges different individuals different prices for the identical item based on estimated willingness to pay.

cards.text: Two friends search for the same hotel room simultaneously and see different room rates based on the smartphone models they use.
cards.explanation: Setting different prices at the same moment based on browsing device is first-degree personalized pricing.

cards.text: Electric utility rates per kilowatt-hour increase for all households during peak late-afternoon air-conditioning hours.
cards.explanation: Time-of-use pricing shifts for all consumers together based on aggregate grid demand.

cards.text: An online retailer quotes higher prices for the same headphones to shoppers whose IP addresses map to high-income postal codes.
cards.explanation: Charging different prices for the same product based on individual location data is personalized pricing.

prompt: Each intervention uses one of the five psychological levers of the SHIFT framework (White, Habib, & Hardisty, 2019) to close the green attitude-behavior gap. Identify the lever.

cases.text: A utility bill displays how a household's monthly electricity use compares with that of efficient neighbors on the same street.
cases.explanation: Signaling peer norms uses Social influence to encourage sustainable conservation.

cases.text: A food-delivery app makes 'no disposable plastic cutlery' the pre-selected default option at checkout so repeat orders stay waste-free automatically.
cases.explanation: Making the sustainable choice the default breaks old routines and supports Habit formation.

cases.text: A refillable cleaning brand affirms the buyer's identity as a capable steward and shows how each refill directly cuts household plastic waste.
cases.explanation: Appealing to personal self-concept and self-efficacy activates the Individual self lever.

cases.text: Rather than using bleak guilt appeals, an electric-vehicle campaign emphasizes the pride and immediate driving enjoyment of clean mobility alongside clear carbon-saving facts.
cases.explanation: Pairing positive emotional pride with clear diagnostic information engages Feelings and cognition.

cases.text: Instead of citing abstract global climate projections for the year 2100, a city transit pass translates each commuter trip into local air-quality gains and immediate monthly dollar savings.
cases.explanation: Making abstract, distant environmental outcomes concrete, local, and immediate uses Tangibility.
